messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Leilani sits stiffly in the chair, her security guard uniform looking a size too big for her now. At sixty-one, she had always taken pride in her work, in the quiet authority of her presence as she patrolled the sprawling corporate campus. That was before the accident six months ago. It happened on a Tuesday in late autumn, the sun already low and casting long, deceptive shadows across the access road. She was making her final round in the patrol vehicle when a young man, an intern from the tech division, stepped out from between two parked cars. He was wearing dark clothes, listening to music. Leilani remembers the jolt, the sickening sound, and then a strange, silent clarity as she saw him on the ground. He survived, but with injuries that would alter the course of his life. And in that moment, Leilani’s own life fractured.

The memory of that evening is not a coherent story she can tell. It comes to her as a collection of broken pieces, and the most crucial seconds—the moment just before impact—are a complete blank. This void is what torments her most. The gaps in her recall feel like an accusation, a space where a terrible truth must be hiding. This forces her into a relentless cycle of questioning. At night, in her small apartment, she sits in the dark and goes over and over the details she *can* remember, trying to make them fit, to force the missing piece to appear. Why her? Why that young man? She dwells endlessly on what she must have done wrong, certain that the blank spot conceals a profound failure of attention, a moment of unforgivable negligence. The harder she tries to reconstruct the event to make sense of it, the more the memory itself feels alien, like a filmstrip about a stranger. Sometimes, when a fragment does surface—the sight of his dark jacket, the specific pitch of the engine—she feels utterly numb, a cold detachment that convinces her she must be a monster.

This constant, circular effort to analyse and understand has, in turn, poisoned the memory itself. Her relentless self-blame has cemented the feeling that the memory doesn’t belong to her; it belongs to the careless, evil woman she now believes herself to be. The act of dwelling on her perceived wrongdoing seems to reinforce the emotional hollowness, pushing the actual experience further away. The more she tries to grasp it, the more it fragments and slips through her fingers, leaving only the profound sense of guilt and the maddening blankness. The memory is no longer an event that happened to her, but a puzzle she has failed to solve, and each failure confirms her culpability. This loop has become the engine of her days and nights, a closed circuit of a fragmented past fueling a punishing present.

Her work, once a source of stability, is now a landscape of torment. Every time she gets in the patrol vehicle, her hands tremble. The sight of an employee walking through the parking lot at dusk sends a jolt of panic through her chest. She has been written up twice for being late on her rounds, her focus shattered by the internal monologue of self-recrimination. She has stopped going to the small church she attended for years, feeling she has no right to be there. The isolation has grown absolute. She came to therapy after her supervisor suggested a leave of absence, a suggestion she heard as the final confirmation of her failure. She is terrified that she will never escape the loop inside her own head, but what she fears most is that if she ever does remember those missing seconds, they will prove that she is exactly the monster she has come to believe she is.
